milestones.title: Portuguese ships reach the port of Kalapa
milestones.detail: In March 1513 the Portuguese captain at Malacca sent four ships to Java. Tomé Pires, writing in 1512-1515, described Calapa as the most important port of the Sunda Kingdom.
milestones.source: Pires, Suma Oriental (1990 reprint), pp. xxv, 172, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta

milestones.title: Sunda-Portuguese treaty at Kalapa
milestones.detail: On 21 August 1522 the Sunda Kingdom concluded a treaty with Portugal that allowed the Portuguese to build a fortress at Kalapa. A stone padrão marking the treaty survives in the National Museum.
milestones.source: Pires, Suma Oriental (1990 reprint), p. 172, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta

milestones.title: Kalapa conquered and becomes Jayakarta
milestones.detail: Islamic forces captured Kalapa on 22 June 1527, the date Jakarta celebrates as its founding. The town became a dependency of Banten and was recorded by Europeans as Jacatra.

milestones.title: VOC destroys Jayakarta and founds Batavia
milestones.detail: Jan Pieterszoon Coen returned with reinforcements in May 1619, razed Jayakarta and made the site the Dutch East India Company's Asian headquarters, named Batavia.
milestones.source: Ricklefs (2001), A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200, p. 35, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batavia,_Dutch_East_Indies

milestones.title: Mataram besieges Batavia; the city is walled
milestones.detail: Sultan Agung of Mataram began a siege on 27 August 1628 and attacked again in 1629. After the sieges failed, a moat and city wall were built that enclosed Batavia completely.

milestones.title: Massacre of Batavia's Chinese residents
milestones.detail: About ten thousand Chinese were killed between 9 and 22 October 1740. The survivors were moved the next year to Glodok, outside the city walls.

milestones.title: Government moves south to Weltevreden
milestones.detail: Governor-General Daendels decided to leave the dilapidated, unhealthy Old Town and built a new centre on the Weltevreden estate further south, giving Batavia two centres.

milestones.title: British occupation under Raffles
milestones.detail: British forces took over the government of Java in 1811. The Dutch returned to rule in 1816.

milestones.title: Railway to Buitenzorg completed
milestones.detail: The city's first railway was begun in 1869, the same year horse trams were introduced, and the line from Batavia to Buitenzorg (Bogor) was completed in 1873.

milestones.title: Tanjung Priok harbour completed
milestones.detail: A new harbour at Tanjung Priok, begun in 1877 as shipping and trade with Europe grew, was completed in 1886.

milestones.title: Meester Cornelis absorbed into Batavia
milestones.detail: The neighbouring municipality of Meester Cornelis (now Jatinegara) was included in the city in 1935.

milestones.title: Japanese occupation; Batavia renamed Jakarta
milestones.detail: Batavia fell to Japanese forces on 5 March 1942. The occupation authorities renamed the city Jakarta.

milestones.title: Indonesian independence proclaimed in Jakarta
milestones.detail: Independence was proclaimed in Jakarta on 17 August 1945.

milestones.title: City area enlarged from 182 to 530 sq km
milestones.detail: In March 1950, after the recognition of Indonesian sovereignty, Jakarta's area was increased from 182 to 530 square kilometres. The added districts were rural and sparsely populated.

milestones.title: Jakarta hosts the Fourth Asian Games
milestones.detail: The 1962 Asian Games were used to complete new landmarks, including the Senayan sports complex, Hotel Indonesia and the Thamrin-Sudirman avenue.

milestones.title: First metro line opens
milestones.detail: Phase 1 of the Jakarta MRT, from Lebak Bulus to Bundaran HI, was officially opened on 24 March 2019.

notes: Start date: the site at the mouth of the Ciliwung was the Sunda Kingdom's port of Kalapa (Sunda Kelapa) before the events usually given as the city's founding. The earliest securely dated document that describes the port town itself is Tomé Pires's Suma Oriental (written 1512-1515; Portuguese ships called in 1513), so 1513 is used as the earliest documented settlement. The port is certainly older, but no dated source for its founding was found; the 13th-century Chinese Zhu Fan Zhi describes a harbour of Sunda that is not securely identified with Kalapa, and the mid-5th-century Tugu inscription found in North Jakarta documents river works in the area, not a town. The city's official anniversary is 22 June 1527 (conquest of Kalapa, traditionally the renaming to Jayakarta, although surviving records do not confirm who led it or the renaming), and the colonial city of Batavia dates from 1619. The start date is therefore contested between 1513 (used here), 1527 and 1619. Population: no figure was found for Kalapa or Jayakarta, so the series starts in 1673; the app should show no reliable estimate from 1513 to 1673. Figures for 1673-1850 are Chandler's estimates for Batavia. From 1880 the figures are colonial counts as reported in secondary sources, and they do not share one boundary: the 1920 figure (306,000) and the 1930 figure (533,000) are larger than the municipal totals quoted elsewhere (253,800 and 435,000), which suggests they include the adjoining Meester Cornelis area that was merged into Batavia in 1935, but the pages consulted do not say so explicitly. The original 1920 and 1930 census volumes were not consulted. Forbes (2004) also gives 823,000 for 1948, which conflicts with 847,483 for 1945 (Twang) and 1,340,625 for 1949 (Merrillees); it was left out. Chandler's 1893 (110,000), 1900 (115,000) and 1925 (290,000) estimates were left out in favour of the counts nearby. Landmarks: no sourced height was found for the pre-1800 buildings of Old Batavia (the 1710 Stadhuis, now the Jakarta History Museum; Gereja Sion, 1695; Kota Intan Bridge, 1628), for Hotel Indonesia or for Gelora Bung Karno Stadium, so they are omitted; the oldest landmark with a sourced height is the 1839 harbour tower. The Selamat Datang and Dirgantara monuments were omitted because the sources give inconsistent or partial heights. Skyscraper heights and years are from the CTBUH Skyscraper Center.
